## The puzzle

```{=html}
<div class="concise-only">
```

After the 28 February 2026 strikes, Saudi Arabia and the UAE pushed Trump — privately and publicly — to continue the war until Iran's regime fell. Yet all five GCC states declined US asks for military support to reopen Hormuz: Saudi denied airbase use, Qatar lobbied Washington against Gulf bases, Kuwait stayed silent. They wanted the war won. They would not pay to win it. Why?

```{=html}
</div>
<div class="deep-only">
```

Within 48 hours of the 28 February 2026 strikes, an unusual pattern surfaced. The two Sunni Gulf monarchies with the deepest US security relationships — Saudi Arabia and the UAE — were *privately* and *publicly* pushing Trump to continue the war until Iran's regime collapsed. Yet both of them, plus Qatar, Kuwait, and Bahrain, declined repeated US asks for military support to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi denied use of Prince Sultan Airbase. Qatar's Emir lobbied Washington against using Gulf bases within 48 hours of war initiation. Kuwait sat on its hands.

So they wanted the war won. They would not pay to win it. Why?

```{=html}
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="concise-only">
```

::: {.bottom-line}
**Bottom line.** *Forward-looking risk minimization under uncertainty about whether Iran survives.* A weakened-but-surviving Iran retaliates against accessible Gulf targets — so the Gulf wants Iran finished. Visible alignment raises future-target risk if Iran survives — so MBS pushes privately, UAE publicly. Four secondary mechanisms ([2023 détente]{.gloss data-gloss="saudi-iran-2023-rapprochement"}, [Vision 2030]{.gloss data-gloss="vision-2030"}, [Yemen lesson]{.gloss data-gloss="yemen-lesson"}, omnibalancing) explain cross-state variation — not the underlying pattern.
:::

```{=html}
</div>
<div class="deep-only">
```

::: {.bottom-line}
**Bottom line.** The single mechanism that resolves the paradox is *forward-looking risk minimization under uncertainty about whether Iran survives the war.* A "weakened but not destroyed" Iran will retaliate against accessible Gulf targets, so the Gulf wants Iran finished. But visible alignment raises future target priority for an Iran that *does* survive — so MBS pushes privately and lets UAE be the public voice. Both halves of the paradox come from the same calculus. Four secondary mechanisms (omnibalancing, the [2023 China-brokered détente]{.gloss data-gloss="saudi-iran-2023-rapprochement"}, [Vision 2030]{.gloss data-gloss="vision-2030"} economic exposure, the [Yemen lesson]{.gloss data-gloss="yemen-lesson"}) explain *which* Gulf state is more or less constrained — not *why* the underlying pattern exists.
:::

## Methodology — the eight-step protocol used here

This chapter applies the project's standard protocol: (1) pre-write a prior; (2) corpus passage extraction; (3) think-tank cross-check; (4) opposing steel-mans; (5) pre-DA synthesis; (6) hostile devil's advocate; (7) reconcile; (8) source-confidence tier audit + Bayesian framing + pre-mortem. After protocol completion, an **external corpus review** against an independently-prepared question briefing surfaced an empirical-premise correction (the canonical "March 16 Trump-GCC bilateral call" was not a bilateral diplomatic ask; it was Trump's March 14–16 Truth Social broadcasts to international consumers) and a stronger single-mechanism account that strictly improved on the multi-mechanism reconciliation. The corrected synthesis is below.
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage1"}
[**Three opening hypotheses.** (1) Textbook [*free-riding*]{.gloss data-gloss="olson-zeckhauser"} — small allies under-contribute. (2) Constrained regime preservation — Sunni monarchies can't openly fight a sectarian war. (3) Iran's strategy — strikes on every GCC capital regardless of contribution fit coercive escalation, not retaliation deterrence.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**Three opening hypotheses, each making different per-state predictions.**

The textbook reading is [*free-riding*]{.gloss data-gloss="olson-zeckhauser"} (Olson & Zeckhauser, 1966): in alliances of formal equals sharing a security public good, small members rationally under-contribute, expecting the larger ally to bear the cost — NATO during the Cold War is the canonical case. Applied here, every GCC state should under-contribute equally; the prediction is *uniform* across states, which already fits poorly with the cross-state variation we observe (Saudi denying airspace, UAE providing basing, Qatar mediating, Bahrain detaining its own Shia, Kuwait silent).

The second reading is *constrained regime preservation* — Sunni monarchies with restive Shia populations cannot openly fight a Sunni-Shia regional war without risking domestic mobilization. This predicts sharp cross-state variation: **Bahrain** (≈ 70 % Shia ruled by a Sunni minority, with the US 5th Fleet on its soil) is the most constrained; **Kuwait** (≈ 30 % Shia, plus an active parliament that would have to consent to combat) is next; **Saudi** has a restive Shia minority concentrated in the Eastern Province; **UAE** and **Qatar** have smaller Shia populations and so face less domestic constraint on visible alignment.

The third reading is *response to Iran's strategy*: Iran attacked every GCC capital regardless of whether they contributed. **UAE** absorbed the heaviest fire (> 150 missiles, 500+ drones); **Qatar** lost LNG export capacity (QatarEnergy declared force majeure on 24 March); **Bahrain** was hit despite domestic Shia anger about the US presence; **Saudi** facilities were struck. Free-rider theory predicts Iran would target only contributors; coercive-escalation theory predicts strikes on everyone, designed to break GCC collective-action capacity.
:::
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage2"}
[**Free-riding fails on three counts.** Iran attacked all GCC capitals regardless of contribution (offensive escalation, not deterrence). Saudi airspace denial *predates* the war — a structural position, not bargaining. And Gulf-US is a [hierarchical clientelist relationship]{.gloss data-gloss="lake-hierarchy"}, not an alliance of equals — clients can constrain patron requests.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**The free-rider reading breaks on three pieces of evidence — and each one points at a specific Gulf state.**

*Iran attacked all GCC capitals*, contributing or not. This fits Schelling's [*threat that leaves something to chance*]{.gloss data-gloss="schelling-something-to-chance"} — a coercive gambit deploying force in ways neither side can fully control, designed to break GCC collective-action capacity rather than punish contributors. **UAE** bore the heaviest cost (> 150 missiles, 500+ drones in the war's first three weeks); **Qatar's** LNG capacity was knocked out; **Bahrain** was hit despite the US 5th Fleet's presence (and the domestic Shia anger that presence already generates); even **Saudi** facilities were struck. A retaliation-only reading predicts Iran would target only contributors; the empirical pattern fits coercion better — the gambit is to make every GCC ruler feel the cost simultaneously, foreclosing any quiet bilateral siding with Washington.

*Saudi airspace denial pre-dated the war.* On 30 January 2026 a senior GCC official told Fox News that Saudi "wouldn't allow airspace to be used in a war Saudi Arabia is not a part of." This was a structural position, not a wartime bargain over costs — and it applied specifically to **Saudi** (the **UAE** provided basing access throughout, and **Qatar** hosted Al Udeid for non-Iran operations). Free-rider theory predicts states should reluctantly grant basing in exchange for security; structural denial isn't free-riding, it's principled refusal.

*The underlying relationship is not an alliance of equals* (the model Olson-Zeckhauser was built on, designed for NATO). It is a [hierarchical clientelist relationship]{.gloss data-gloss="lake-hierarchy"} in which the small state cedes authority over basing rights and foreign-policy alignment in exchange for security guarantees, and the patron is constrained by what it can demand without violating the implicit bargain. **Saudi** airspace denial is a *clientelist signal* — the patron (the US) requested action without consultation or burden-sharing on cost — not under-contribution within an intact alliance. The frame matters: Olson-Zeckhauser predicts free-riding everywhere; Lake's hierarchy predicts client *resistance* when patron requests damage client interests, exactly what we observed in Riyadh and Doha.
:::
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage3"}
[**DA-corrected synthesis: four mechanisms.** Lake's hierarchy + [omnibalancing]{.gloss data-gloss="omnibalancing"} + 2023 détente + Vision 2030 + Yemen lesson, each operative for a different Gulf sub-set. This explained *which* states were more or less constrained — not *why* the pattern existed.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**The DA-corrected synthesis: four mechanisms, each operative for a different sub-set of Gulf states.** Replacing Olson-Zeckhauser with Lake's hierarchy fixed the structural framing; four further mechanisms then explain the cross-state variation.

*[Omnibalancing]{.gloss data-gloss="omnibalancing"}* (David 1991; Gause 2003/4): leaders of fragile states balance against the larger of internal and external threats. Sunni monarchies face *both* Iran externally and a domestic Shia population that could be mobilized by a sectarian war. The mechanism is **load-bearing for Bahrain** (≈ 70 % Shia ruled by a Sunni minority; 350+ wartime detentions per Carnegie / Al-Monitor / Middle East Eye reporting; some Bahraini Shia openly cheered US base attacks per Stimson), **significant for Kuwait** (smaller Shia population but a parliament whose consent would be required for combat participation), and **present in Saudi** (restive Eastern Province). It is **least binding for the UAE** (small Shia population, strong internal-security apparatus).

*The [2023 China-brokered Saudi-Iran rapprochement]{.gloss data-gloss="saudi-iran-2023-rapprochement"}* (10 March 2023): Riyadh and Tehran restored diplomatic relations after seven years severed, with China as the broker. Joining a Hormuz fight in 2026 would torch this standing infrastructure — and lose Beijing's good will, foreclosing the Saudi hedging option between Washington and Beijing. The mechanism is **load-bearing for Saudi** specifically; the UAE's bilateral with Iran was thinner and the cost of breaking it is correspondingly smaller.

*[Vision 2030]{.gloss data-gloss="vision-2030"} / FDI risk*: Saudi Vision 2030 (announced by MBS in 2016) and the UAE's parallel diversification strategy both depend on sustained foreign direct investment, expat professional labor, and a stable regional security environment. Visible escalation against Iran threatens all three: investors flee, expats leave, tourism collapses. MBS reportedly turned from pro-war to off-ramp-seeking once these costs became tangible. **Operative for Saudi and UAE**; effectively absent for Bahrain, Kuwait, Qatar, Oman.

*The [Yemen lesson]{.gloss data-gloss="yemen-lesson"}*: Saudi led a coalition into Yemen in March 2015 and spent seven years failing to defeat the Houthis. The structural conclusion — that a regional war the Gulf cannot definitively finish becomes an existential trap — is **the dominant Saudi internal explanation for restraint** on direct Iran combat in 2026, with secondary effects for the UAE (which exited the Yemen front in 2019).

The four together explain *which* Gulf state is more or less constrained: **Bahrain** by omnibalancing, **Saudi** by all four (détente + Vision 2030 + Yemen + clientelist), **UAE** primarily by Vision 2030 modulated by less omnibalancing exposure, **Qatar** and **Kuwait** by their distinct mediator and parliamentary constraints. They do not yet explain *why* the underlying puzzle — wanting the war won while refusing to pay to win it — exists in the first place.
:::
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage4"}
[**Single-mechanism account.** Ibish's *post-war retaliation risk* explains both halves: a surviving Iran retaliates → push for regime change; visible alignment raises future-target risk → decline visible platform. The four DA mechanisms become modifiers explaining cross-state variation. Strictly better: same predictive power, plus an account of why.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**The single-mechanism account: [Ibish post-war retaliation risk]{.gloss data-gloss="ibish-post-war-retaliation-risk"}.** A briefing-review pass surfaced a stronger reading. Hussein Ibish (Arab Gulf States Institute in Washington, March 2026) argued that Sunni Gulf monarchies face one asymmetric forward-looking calculation. A "weakened but not destroyed" Iran will retaliate against accessible Gulf targets — so the Gulf wants Iran finished. But visible alignment raises future-target priority if Iran *does* survive — so the monarchies push the war privately while declining to be its public platform. Both halves of the paradox come from the same calculus, and the calculus *predicts the cross-state pattern observed*, not just the aggregate behavior:

- **Saudi Arabia** — MBS pushes for regime change in private US channels (per New York Times and Washington Post reporting on US officials' read-outs of Mar-a-Lago meetings) but declines to be the public platform. The 2023 détente and Vision 2030 amplify this: he *especially* wants to avoid public alignment because both his hedging-with-Beijing and his FDI-dependent economy take damage if Iran survives and remembers.
- **UAE** — Anwar Gargash's framing of the war as a "permanent state of threat" is the public voice. The UAE has already paid the heaviest cost in Iranian missile fire, faces less omnibalancing constraint, and has alternative bypass capacity (Habshan-Fujairah ~ 1.5 mb/d) — so the calculus comes out differently: visible alignment is more affordable.
- **Bahrain** — most domestically constrained; stays quietest. Omnibalancing dominates; under Ibish's calculus, Bahrain has the strongest reason to keep all alignment private.
- **Qatar** — the [biased-mediator]{.gloss data-gloss="kydd-biased-mediator"} role (Kydd 2003) gives plausible deniability and a substantive function. Qatar's Emir lobbied Washington against using Gulf bases within 48 hours of war initiation — privately credible, publicly denying platform.
- **Oman** — Iran reportedly chose not to strike Oman, which fits Kydd's biased-mediator framework: Oman's long-standing closeness to Iran makes its messages credible to Tehran in a way no neutral state's could be.

The four DA-derived mechanisms (omnibalancing, 2023 détente, Vision 2030, Yemen lesson) are recast as *modifiers* of the per-state calculus — they explain *how strongly* each state weights the calculation, not whether the calculation is taking place. This is strictly better than the four-mechanism reconciliation: same predictive power for cross-state variation, plus a coherent account of why the underlying behavior pattern exists.
:::
:::

:::

[**Reading the chart.** Each row is one mechanism. The light grey bar shows posterior P(operative) — how likely the mechanism is at play. The colored foreground bar shows posterior P(load-bearing) — how much of the puzzle the mechanism actually explains. Color encodes the [tier badge]{.gloss data-gloss="source-confidence-tier"}: green = T1 (multi-source verified), yellow = T2 (single-source named), red = T3 (inference from evidence), grey = T4 (conjecture). The dashed blue line at 0.5 marks the load-bearing threshold; above the line means the mechanism is doing more than chance work in the synthesis. The headline finding — **M0 at 65% P(load-bearing)** — is *not* T1, because Ibish's specific framing has not yet been independently corroborated in the wider think-tank literature. Treat it as the best current single-mechanism account, not as established.]{.deep-only}

[Olson-Zeckhauser was designed for alliances of formal equals (NATO). The Gulf-US relationship is an asymmetric clientelist relationship — a different game-theoretic object with different equilibria. ### Figure 4 — Source-confidence tier breakdown

Of the synthesis's load-bearing claims:

- **[T1]{.tier .tier-1} multi-source verified:** Iran attacked all GCC capitals; Bahrain 350+ detentions in war period; QatarEnergy LNG force majeure (March 24); 2023 Saudi-Iran rapprochement was China-brokered; Petroline / Habshan-Fujairah capacities; Saudi airspace position predates the war.
- **[T2]{.tier .tier-2} single-source named:** UAE OPEC+ exit; Saudi-UAE coordination fractures; Iran chose Oman for mediation; Trump's "biggest surprise" framing; Vision 2030 / NEOM constraint on Saudi hawkishness.
- **[T3]{.tier .tier-3} inference from evidence:** Iran's strategy as offensive coercive gambit (rather than retaliation deterrent); domestic-Shia-population threat as binding constraint on Sunni monarchies; GCC bureaucratic incoherence reflects intelligence-vs-foreign-ministry gap.
- **[T4]{.tier .tier-4} conjecture:** none in the load-bearing path post-revision.

The biggest inferential claim ([T3]{.tier .tier-3}) is the reframing of Iran's strategy as offensive gambit rather than deterrent. This is a methodological choice (reading the same evidence through different framework) rather than a factual claim. The omnibalancing/domestic-Shia-threat claim ([T3]{.tier .tier-3}) does substantial analytical work and is flagged for further verification with primary MENA-studies sources.

## Pre-mortem {#pre-mortem}

If this synthesis is wrong, the most likely failure modes are:

1. **Underweighting Iranian strategic agency.** M5 (Iran's offensive gambit) is partly inferential. If Iran was actually retaliating defensively rather than coercing strategically, the equilibrium reading is right but the mechanism label is wrong.
2. **The four secondary mechanisms may be redundant rather than independent.** Omnibalancing, 2023 détente, Vision 2030, and Yemen lesson all point toward Sunni Gulf restraint — they may be different symptoms of the same underlying structural condition (Sunni monarchies in a multi-ethnic region with FDI-dependent economies and recent failed-war experience). Treating them as independent risks double-counting.
3. **Over-confidence in the omnibalancing replacement of free-riding.** Gause's 2003/4 *Security Studies* article is referenced indirectly via published summaries and engagement in secondary scholarship — the original paywalled article was not directly used. If Gause's actual argument differs from the reconstruction, there is a gap that the chapter cannot close without primary access.
4. **The DA's framework swap may itself be an over-correction.** Lake's hierarchy predicts client constraints on patron action, but the empirical record (Gulf states accepting US protection across decades; granting basing rights; coordinating on sanctions) shows substantial cooperation that pure clientelism would predict less of. Both free-riding and clientelist constraint may operate.

## Pre-1979 historical lineage

The Q12.4 paradox — MBS-private + UAE-public pushing regime change while declining basing — must be read against a **47-year inversion of pre-1979 Iran-as-Gulf-gendarme reality**. Through the Pahlavi period (especially 1953-1979), Iran was the Persian Gulf's hegemonic guarantor on US/Israeli terms: tacit Iran-Israel-Turkey "Periphery Doctrine" alignment against Arab nationalist threats; **1971 Pahlavi annexation of Abu Musa, Greater Tunb, Lesser Tunb** (still UAE territorial dispute today); **1973-1975 Dhofar intervention** on behalf of Oman against PFLO insurgency; **1975 Algiers Accord** resolving Iran-Iraq border on terms humiliating to Iraq (Saddam tore this up to start the 1980 Iran-Iraq war); US-supplied AWACS, F-14s, F-4s; Iran was the largest US arms customer in the world by mid-1970s.

That regional posture inverted in 1979 — but the institutional memory persisted in Gulf elites for 47 years. The current GCC behavior — accept some Iran-containment costs but not all — is the inheritance of a state that was once their hegemonic enforcer and is now their adversary. The 2026 paradox (push for regime change privately; decline basing publicly) is partly the calculation Q12.4's load-bearing mechanism (Ibish post-war retaliation risk) names; it is also partly the long memory of having been on the receiving end of Iran's regional projection in the 1970s — when annexation, intervention, and humiliating border settlements were live operational facts, not historical curiosities. The Saudi-Iran 2023 China-brokered rapprochement is the most recent expression of a Gulf hedge against future Iranian regional reassertion under that 47-year-old institutional memory.

**Full pre-1979 context**: [Historical roots](../historical-roots/index.qmd).

## How to read the tier badges

[T1]{.tier .tier-1} **Multi-source verified.** Independent corroboration from at least two distinct sources of different type (e.g., a wire service plus a peer-reviewed analysis).

[T2]{.tier .tier-2} **Single-source named.** Reported by one named source. Not yet independently corroborated.

[T3]{.tier .tier-3} **Inference from evidence.** A reading of empirical evidence under a chosen analytical framework. The factual base is supported but the inferential leap is the analyst's.

[T4]{.tier .tier-4} **Conjecture.** A working hypothesis not yet supported by either named source or strong inference.
